episode_title: The Oranges and the Colonies: A Royal Reckoning
description: A study commissioned by King Willem-Alexander finds the Dutch royal family backed colonialism for centuries and profited by about €576 million. Prime Minister Jetten rules out new reparations. Also today: inflation and the G7's emergency diesel release, a court ruling on family reunification, tighter mortgages for older buyers, a planned vape tax, the Golden Calf winners, the fight over Meta's camera glasses, and 75 years of Dutch television.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: The Dutch royal family backed colonialism for centuries, and earned the equivalent of about five hundred and seventy-six million euros from it. That's the verdict of a study the King asked for himself. He calls it heartbreaking. The prime minister says there'll be no new reparations.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: It's Saturday, the third of October. I'm Sam.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: And I'm Maya. This is Dutch Daily Briefing.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: We start with that study of the Oranges, as the royal family's known, and their colonial past.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: On Friday, in Leiden, King Willem-Alexander received a two-thousand-page study he'd asked for and paid for himself. The lead researcher, Gert Oostindie, doesn't soften it. Every stadtholder, king and queen, at least up to Queen Wilhelmina, gave colonialism what he calls 'active and unscrupulous' support. That includes slavery, and the violent crushing of uprisings.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: And they profited. In today's money, close to five hundred and seventy-six million euros. Almost all of it came from the VOC, the Dutch East India Company, and from the Dutch East Indies, now Indonesia.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Is that money still in the family?

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Very little of it, the researchers say. William the Fifth fled the country penniless in 1795, and later fortunes vanished into investments in Tsarist Russia. One grim detail: they made almost nothing from the transatlantic slave trade. Not out of principle. The West India Company just lost them money.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: But they didn't usually set the policy.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Mostly not. This is a constitutional monarchy, so they backed colonialism more than they shaped it. The exception was King William the First, who largely ran colonial policy himself, and in 1828 looked for ways around laws against the slave trade. The study calls Queen Wilhelmina the most imperialist. In 1947, during the fight against Indonesian independence, she wrote that she had no objection to 'police actions'. Criticism from the palace only began with Queen Juliana, in 1948.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: The King called the findings 'heartbreaking and confronting'. He said, 'I cannot change the past, but I can make a positive contribution to the present and the future.' He didn't mention any financial repair. And Prime Minister Rob Jetten ruled out new reparations, pointing to the two hundred million euros set aside in 2023 for awareness, remembrance and education.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Reactions are split. NiNsee, the national institute on Dutch slavery and its legacy, welcomed the report and wants talks on repair. A foundation for Indigenous people from Suriname and the Caribbean says they've been overlooked again. And activist Mitchell Esajas of The Black Archives sent back his royal honour, saying words about reconciliation aren't enough.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: The King calls the report not a conclusion, but a call to action. Plenty of people now want to see what that action looks like.

segments.title: Inflation and the G7 diesel release

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Now, inflation, and if you've filled up a car lately, you already know the culprit.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Dutch inflation rose to three point four percent in September, according to a first estimate from CBS, the statistics bureau. Fuel and heating cost almost fourteen percent more than a year ago. Groceries actually got a bit cheaper.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Enjoy that while it lasts. CBS's chief economist says high energy prices usually reach shop shelves about six months later. Though he's not expecting a spike like 2022.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Across the eurozone, inflation's at three point eight percent, the highest in three years. And then there's diesel.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Right. The G7 agreed to release up to a hundred million barrels of diesel and crude oil from emergency reserves over four months, with a lot of the diesel coming in the first twenty days.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Why now?

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Pressure from Donald Trump. He'd threatened to ban US diesel exports to bring prices down at home before the midterms, and Europe now gets much of its diesel from the US. European diesel futures fell about eight percent on the news.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: The Netherlands isn't in the G7, but it's already tapping its own reserves under an earlier international deal from March. On Thursday the cabinet released another batch, mostly diesel and petrol. No word yet on whether it'll chip in more now. And there's no new fuel tax cut. The cabinet's just phasing out the existing discount more slowly next year.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: So advisory pump prices are still above two euros seventy a litre, though the average people actually pay is lower. Worth watching what diesel does over the next few weeks.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: To a court ruling now, on refugees bringing their families to the Netherlands.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Stricter rules took effect in June under the EU's new asylum pact. The question was: do they also apply to applications filed before that?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: And the district court in The Hague says yes. The case was brought by two Syrians with what's called subsidiary protection.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: That's the key term. It means you're not recognised as a refugee, but it isn't safe for you to go home. Under the new two-status system, people with subsidiary protection have to wait two years before they can apply to bring family over, and they need housing big enough for the whole family.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: And the law has no transition period, so those rules hit applications that were already pending. When it took effect, more than nineteen thousand people were waiting on a decision from the IND, the immigration service. It's not clear how many of them have subsidiary protection.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: The court admitted the effects can be serious, especially for people who applied under the old rules. But it found no breach of higher law or general legal principles.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: The Syrians' lawyer will appeal, and the final word goes to the Council of State, the country's top administrative court. No date yet for that ruling.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Mortgages next, and some bad news if you're in your fifties.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Rabobank and ABN Amro are cutting how much older buyers can borrow. From next March, Rabobank will count your expected pension income starting fifteen years before retirement, instead of ten. So from age fifty-two.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: And pensions are usually lower than salaries, so the maximum loan shrinks. Rabobank will also factor in life expectancy. From eighty-five, you can borrow at most seventy percent of your home's value.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: ABN Amro follows this December, with a cap of fifty percent at that age.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: It all comes from new guidance by DNB, the Dutch central bank. Any part of a loan that outlasts your life expectancy is treated like interest-only debt, to be repaid mainly by selling the house.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Who's hit hardest?

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Self-employed people with little pension saved. The data firm IEX calculated that someone relying only on the state pension may qualify for a mortgage of about a hundred thousand euros.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: If you keep your current mortgage unchanged, none of this affects you, but refinancing does. ING hasn't announced anything yet, though others in the sector expect more lenders to follow.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Vaping now, and it's about to get pricier. Just not for a while.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: The government plans an excise tax on vapes and refills from January 2029, on top of the twenty-one percent VAT. The rate isn't set yet, but the aim is to make vapes about as expensive as tobacco.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: This is State Secretary for Finance Eelco Eerenberg of D66. He's a junior minister in charge of taxes, and he says it's shocking how many young people vape.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: In the latest schools survey, more than one in five pupils aged twelve to sixteen had tried a vape.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: He also says 'the health of our children cannot wait for Brussels.' The EU proposed its own vape tax, but tax rules need all twenty-seven countries to agree, and in June finance ministers dropped it from their agenda.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: If an EU tax does arrive before 2029, the Dutch plan will be withdrawn. And Eerenberg admits vapes are easy to buy online or across the border anyway.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: The bill should reach the Tweede Kamer, the House of Representatives, early next year. And flavoured vapes have been banned since 2024, though in practice that ban's often ignored.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: In Amsterdam, the city's backed off a plan to make Utrechtsestraat one-way.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: That's the busy shopping and restaurant street running from Rembrandtplein down to Frederiksplein. The city called it unsafe and wanted northbound traffic sent through side streets.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: But residents pushed back hard. Neighbourhood groups feared traffic would spill into their streets, challenged the city's figures and did their own counts. Local businesses opposed it too.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: So the city's going smaller: an extra zebra crossing, speed checks, speed bumps, and a crackdown on illegal loading. The district committee for the centre discusses it on Monday, before a final decision.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Score one for the neighbours.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Maya, quick question. Have you seen the film about a teenage boy whose dad runs a low-budget porn business?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Can't say I have. Should I?

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Apparently, yes. It's called Truly Naked, and it just swept the Golden Calves, the Dutch film and TV awards. Think Oscars and Emmys rolled into one, handed out in Utrecht at the end of the Netherlands Film Festival. It won six of its seven nominations, including best film, and best director for Muriel d'Ansembourg. It's her first feature.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: And here's the good news for our listeners: it's in English.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Set in a British seaside town, about how porn shapes teenage lives. It's already streaming, on Pathé Thuis among others.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Then there's Basta, a series about Marco van Basten. Newcomers, he's one of the greatest Dutch footballers ever, the man behind that famous volley in the 1988 European Championship final.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Which is still the Dutch team's only major title. So, no pressure. Basta won three, including best drama series and best actor for Chris Peters. It's on Videoland.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: And the favourite, Joe Speedboot, with nine nominations, went home with just one: best actor for Daan Buringa.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Ouch. And Halina Reijn, who directed Nicole Kidman in Babygirl, got a career award and called herself 'a farmer's girl in Hollywood.'

segments.title: Hans Anders pulls Meta's camera glasses

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Smart glasses now, and one Dutch optician just took them off the shelves.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Hans Anders, the budget optician on just about every Dutch high street, has stopped selling Meta's AI camera glasses, the ones made with Ray-Ban. For now.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Remind me what these things do.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: They look like normal glasses, but they take photos and video hands-free, make calls, play music. There's a little light that flickers while you're recording. They start at four hundred and nineteen euros.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Why pull them?

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: The chain points to the public and political debate. And the critics' nickname for them is 'gluurbril'. Peeping glasses.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Which tells you how that debate's going.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Pretty much. On Tuesday, the abuse victims' support group Offlimits and campaign group The Firewall gave Meta two weeks to stop selling them, saying they make covert filming easy. Otherwise, they'll go to court.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Same day, the Tweede Kamer passed a motion asking the cabinet to further restrict wearing them, with exceptions for medical use. But the cabinet's hesitant. It wants to wait for an EU assessment, expected this autumn.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Meanwhile, if you really want a pair, Pearle, Specsavers, MediaMarkt and Ray-Ban stores are all still selling them. And Hans Anders had only sold limited numbers anyway.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: So not a huge sacrifice. Hans Anders will decide later whether they come back.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Maya, would you pay a third of your yearly income for a television?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Not a chance.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: That's what a set cost when Dutch TV began, seventy-five years ago this week. And there were only about five hundred of them in the whole country.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: So how did people watch?

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Through radio shop windows, or in cafés. Even the royals watched, at Soestdijk Palace. It was a ninety-minute live show from a studio in Bussum.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: And not everyone was thrilled.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Not at all. Prime Minister Willem Drees wanted money spent on housing, and feared TV would distract workers and corrupt the young. Father Kors, who headed the broadcasters, warned on air about its harmful influence.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: On air. Bold. Wait, a priest ran the broadcasters?

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Very Dutch. Society back then was split into pillars: Catholic, Protestant, socialist, liberal, each with its own broadcasters. That's why public TV here is still shared among lots of them. Anyway, what forced the issue was Philips, the Eindhoven electronics company. It threatened to start TV itself, so the government gave in, as a two-year experiment.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Seventy-five years on, a media historian says TV is still 'the dominant medium.' Father Kors would be horrified.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: And if that's got you off the sofa, here's what's on in Amsterdam today. Tonight at the Ziggo Dome in Zuidoost, the Concertgebouw Orchestra plays classical highlights with Iván Fischer conducting, ending with Beethoven's Ninth.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: And the whole arena gets to sing along to the 'Ode to Joy'. There's an optional sing-along rehearsal at seven, and the concert starts at eight.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: I'll be humming. Or, for something cosier, it's the second-to-last day of Camera Japan, the Benelux's biggest Japanese film festival, at LAB111 in Oud-West. Anime, arthouse and classics, plus food and music, from half past twelve. Times may shift, so check their website.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: And this morning, there's a free antiques, curiosities and vintage market at the Oosterkerk, in the eastern city centre, until five. One day only.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: That's the show for today. I'm Sam.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: And I'm Maya. This has been Dutch Daily Briefing. Have a lovely weekend, and we'll talk soon.
